Two walks of the unallocated space table still use eloc after the walk has reached the end of the table. udf_table_prealloc_blocks() looks for a free extent starting at first_block and decides whether it found one by comparing eloc with first_block after the walk. If the table's list ends in a continuation descriptor that leads to an empty allocation extent, eloc is then the block of that allocation extent, which is in use, and if that is first_block, the block is handed out as preallocation. Once udf_discard_prealloc() no longer frees the wrong block, this is what still makes fsx in generic/091 and generic/263 read back bad data on a table, in about one run in four. Only take the extent if the walk stopped at it. When udf_table_free_blocks() cannot merge the freed blocks into an existing extent, it appends a new one and sets only its block number, so the partition reference comes from whatever eloc held after the walk, and with long allocation descriptors it is written to disk. For a table without extents, eloc was never set. Take the partition reference from the freed blocks instead. Short allocation descriptors do not store the partition reference, which is why this half remains a latent long-descriptor fix rather than a reproduced failure.

t: MIPS: sgi-ip32: Leave MACE PCI control alone in config accesses
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: MIPS: sgi-ip32: Leave MACE PCI control alone in config accesses mace_pci_read_config() clears the master abort interrupt enable in the MACE PCI control register around each config read. A register read followed by two register writes can hang CRIME 1.1 under DMA load. Ack master aborts in the error register instead, and follow every write with a read so back-to-back accesses cannot form that sequence.

t: srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: srcu: Add list_splice_init_srcu() list_splice_init_rcu() makes a list look empty to new readers, waits for the current ones with the given sync function, and only then links the entries into the new list. The sync function takes no argument, so it can wait for RCU readers but not for the readers of an srcu_struct. Passing synchronize_rcu() for a list read under SRCU still builds, but leaves SRCU readers on the entries while the last one's next pointer is moved onto the new list head. nvme_remove_namespaces() does this today. Add list_splice_init_srcu(), which waits for the readers of the given srcu_struct instead.

t: nvme: wait for SRCU readers before splicing the namespace list
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme: wait for SRCU readers before splicing the namespace list Readers walk ctrl->namespaces under ctrl->srcu, and some of them sleep there, e.g. nvme_wait_freeze() waiting for I/O to drain. nvme_remove_namespaces() moves the list onto its on-stack ns_list with list_splice_init_rcu(), which only waits for RCU readers before relinking the entries. A reader still on the last namespace then follows its next pointer to ns_list instead of ctrl->namespaces and treats the stack as a namespace. Deleting a controller while a Format NVM passthrough waits for a delayed read on the last namespace gives: BUG: KASAN: stack-out-of-bounds in nvme_wait_freeze+0x102/0x120 Read of size 8 at addr ff110001d2f3fc38 by task nvme/4413 Call Trace: nvme_wait_freeze nvme_passthru_start nvme_submit_user_cmd nvme_user_cmd nvme_dev_ioctl BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff8af04850 Use list_splice_init_srcu() instead, which waits for the SRCU readers. This also takes the RCU grace period out of every controller deletion. Deleting 64 tcp controllers with one namespace each, median of 3 runs on each of two boots per kernel: before after nvme disconnect-all (ms) 3491 / 3509 2996 / 3165 nvme_remove_namespaces() avg (ms) 39.0 / 40.5 31.9 / 34.7

t: sched/fair: Clear throttle state when leaving the fair class
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sched/fair: Clear throttle state when leaving the fair class Task-based CFS bandwidth throttling removes a task's fair sched_entity while the scheduler core still considers the task queued. p->throttled carries the fair-specific state across dequeue/enqueue operations. DEQUEUE_CLASS removes the task from cfs_rq->throttled_limbo_list but retains the bit. If the last finite CFS quota is disabled while the task runs in another class, it is absent from the unthrottle walk and the bit survives. Returning to fair while cfs_bandwidth_used() is false then performs a real fair enqueue with p->throttled still set. After bandwidth is re-enabled, a class-change dequeue treats the stale bit as limbo state and skips __dequeue_task(). p->se.on_rq therefore remains set, and put_prev_task_fair() places the entity in the EEVDF tree while the task moves to RT. On exit, the fair picker can select the TASK_DEAD task. __schedule() then returns to do_task_dead(), which hits BUG(). Keep p->throttled across migrations and group moves, but clear it on DEQUEUE_CLASS because fair-specific state must not outlive fair-class membership. A later return to fair uses the normal enqueue path. That path still respects a throttled cfs_rq. A KASAN, LOCKDEP and DEBUG_LIST v7.3 kernel reproduced the do_task_dead() BUG in 3/3 root and 3/3 delegated uid-1000 runs with CapPrm=CapEff=0 and RLIMIT_RTPRIO=1. The fix passed both matrices plus a 3/3 class-switch control with bandwidth continuously enabled, without a scheduler warning, KASAN report, lockdep splat or crash. An AI coding assistant analyzed the state mismatch and drafted the initial reproducer, fix candidate and this changelog. The source paths, trigger, controls and results were rechecked against the cited revisions.

t: arm64: kexec_file: Fix elf_headers memory leak in retry loop
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: arm64: kexec_file: Fix elf_headers memory leak in retry loop A retry allocates new elf headers and overwrites image->elf_headers, leaking the previous buffer. Free it before assigning. [catalin.marinas@arm.com: drop the redundant NULL check before vfree()]

t: arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers An SDEI event is dispatched by firmware regardless of PSTATE.DAIF, so it can interrupt the kernel where the exception registers are live: - exception entry, before kernel_entry has saved ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and before the C handler has read ESR_EL1/FAR_EL1; - exception return, after kernel_exit has loaded ELR_EL1/SPSR_EL1 and before the ERET. An IRQ or pseudo-NMI cannot arrive there with PSTATE.I set. Firmware saves only x0-x17, PC and PSTATE around an SDEI event, so a synchronous exception taken by the handler overwrites the interrupted context's ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR. do_sdei_event() only notices that ELR changed, and warns. The interrupted context then carries on with the handler's state. A task interrupted on its way into the kernel can be sent SIGILL for the handler's kernel data abort. A task interrupted on its way back to user space ERETs to EL1, at the handler's fixup address, with user registers loaded. With SDEI delivering NMI backtraces, this happens in normal operation. The handler runs show_regs(), which reads through possibly-NULL pointers with the _nofault() accessors. print_worker_info() faults this way for a kworker that is not running a work item, and a single sysrq-l warned once per such kworker. Save ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR in __sdei_handler() before irqentry_nmi_enter(), which can take an exception too, and restore them after irqentry_nmi_exit(). Once they are restored, a nested exception is harmless if its handler is safe in NMI context. That holds for EL1 data aborts on translation, permission and access-flag faults, which never take the mmap lock in NMI context, and for BRK. Warn once, with the syndrome, about any other exception class.

t: x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: x86/mm: Fix global ASID handed out to two processes On AMD CPUs with INVLPGB, two live processes can get the same MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE global ASID value. The two then hit each other's TLB entries, so each can read or corrupt the other's memory. The global ASID space is managed lazily. When a global ASID is freed, its bit is set in the global_asid_freed bitmap. Once the free ASID search reaches the end of the global_asid_used bitmap, a global flush is done to really reclaim the lazily freed global ASIDs. However, the current code can assign the same global ASID to two different processes, if one process is assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE - 1, another process MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, and both stick around (keeping their global ASID numbers in use) until the search wraps around again. At that point a third process could also get assigned MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE. the highest ASID stays in use, so it is not handed out again last_global_asid stays below it, so no reset the clear bits run out find_next_zero_bit() returns MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE global_asid_available > 0, so the failure is not caught MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE is handed out as an ASID A search only looks at the bits below MAX_ASID_AVAILABLE, so it cannot see that this value is in use. The next failed search hands it out again, even if the first process still holds it. The fix used here is to reset the global ASID space after a failed search, and to search again. If that search fails too, no global ASID is handed out. The test for !global_asid_available is removed, because use_global_asid() only calls allocate_global_asid() if global_asid_available > 0. The remaining test is for a condition that should be impossible. [ riel: simplify code, massage changelog and comment ]

t: iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/amd: Force device table to maximum size IOMMU can perform out-of-bounds read of the device table entry (DTE) that is adjacent to the last DTE and falls outside the device table. For example, if the device table can hold 0 to N-1 entries, then the IOMMU can be made to fetch the Nth entry, which falls outside the device table. The device table is owned by the hypervisor (HV) and is assigned in 4KB pages that are contiguous in system physical address (SPA). If the out-of-bound DTE falls on a guest-owned page, then the guest can exploit this bug to setup malicious table walks to corrupt HV pages and/or bring down the system. Note that this bug does not manifest when the device table size is set to its maximum size of 2MB. Therefore, force the device table size to the maximum 2MB on affected processors. These are CPU family 0x17 (Zen1/Zen2) through family 0x1a (Zen5/BRH). This is a mitigation for CVE-2024-21963. kdump reuses the previous kernel's device table only when the size encoded in the IOMMU device-table register matches pci_seg->dev_table_size. A mixed rollout disagrees: the unpatched kernel uses the IVRS-derived size and the patched kernel uses 2MB, so __reuse_device_table() rejects the table. On SNP-capable IOMMUs that rejection panics the kdump kernel. Kernels that both have this patch agree on 2MB and reuse succeeds. Update the production kernel and the crash kernel together.

t: ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ceph: clamp the inline data length in ceph_fill_inline_data() The MDS decides how much inline data to attach to a reply, and the client parses inline_len without any upper bound: ceph_decode_need() only verifies that the message actually carries that many bytes. ceph_fill_inline_data() then copies the data into a single folio with no length check, so a malicious or buggy MDS returning more inline data than the folio can hold writes past its end. Clamp the length to folio_size() so both callers, handle_cap_grant() and fill_inode(), are covered.

t: batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: clear ROAM flag when re-adding a pending local client When a ROAMING_ADV is received for an announced local client, batadv_tt_local_mark_removed() sets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM, queues a DEL|ROAM change and marks the entry as BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING. If the client sends a frame again before the next TTVN commit, batadv_tt_local_add_existing() only clears the PENDING flag and returns early. The ADD cancels the queued DEL, but the entry keeps the ROAM flag: * batadv_is_my_client() reports the client as not served by this node * batadv_tt_local_client_is_roaming() reroutes unicast frames for it to the node which sent the ROAMING_ADV The ROAM flag is only removed with the next frame of the client. Since BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM is set together with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING, it has to be cleared also at the same time with BATADV_TT_CLIENT_PENDING when the client roamed back.

t: batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: batman-adv: tt: only update flags for TT events In the first implementation of the translation table events, it was only possible to announce: * ADD: new locally detected client * DEL: disappeared local client If an ADD event was queued and then a DEL event was queued in the same timeslot, it is valid to destroy both events because nothing actually changed for remode nodes But with commit 3c4f7ab60cc2 ("batman-adv: improve the TT component to support runtime flag changes") and subsequent changes, it could also happen that there are extra ADD events: * ADD: _NEW_ locally detected client * ADD: already existing client with new flags * DEL: disappeared local client The first and the last type of event could in theory still be removed together from the (to be announced) events queue. But if the "update flags" ADD is dropped together with the DEL, it would still leave global translation table of a remote node in the incorrect state - believing that the client didn't disappear. If a detected client was previously announced, a DEL event must only overwrite the "update flags" ADD but the DEL itself must still continue to exist in the (to be anounced) events queue. For now, adjustment of the announced flags is used for everything instead of dropping already queued up events completely. Similarly, a DEL followed by an ADD caused both entries to be deleted. But the new ADD could announce flags changes which were not yet present for the client before it was marked for DELetion. The new ADD must therefore only overwrite the DEL - but still be kept.

t: ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: ata: libata-scsi: reject data-in commands with a data-out buffer SG_IO can submit a data-in SCSI command with DMA_TO_DEVICE. The scatterlist can then contain pages pinned without write access. ata_scsi_rbuf_fill() writes simulated replies to that scatterlist; in the reported case, the copy tried to write the shared zero page and faulted in the kernel. The same mismatch can affect SG_IO commands translated by libata. ZBC IN and GET PHYSICAL ELEMENT STATUS completion handlers can modify the receive buffer even if the drive aborts the command. For ATAPI, the successful INQUIRY completion also rewrites the buffer in atapi_fixup_inquiry(). Reject these mismatched commands before the buffer is written or the command is issued. Report ABORTED COMMAND / DATA IN BUFFER ERROR because the CDB itself can be valid; the supplied transfer direction is wrong.

t: iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommu/arm-smmu-v3: Handle ARM erratum for CONT under invalidation with SVA The erratum (MMU-700: #3777127, S3: #3673557) deals with under invalidation of a CONT PTE grouping in the SMMU. The recommended work around is to use a range invalidation that spans the entire CONT. The only user of CONT in the kernel right now is through SVA sharing a CPU page table that contains a CONT created by the mm. Previously it was thought that this errata was dealt with because the driver always uses range invalidation. However, there is a subtle detail in the errata that the invalidation range must fully enclose the entire CONT for it to work. It seems that two sequential range invalidations, with a split point falling inside a CONT grouping, will not prevent the errata. The SMMU's range invalidation generation algorithm does not produce a single invalidation for a single SVA invalidation request, nor does the mm carefully align the SVA invalidation ranges to accommodate the splitting of the invalidation into several ranges. Thus, when processing a SVA invalidation, the range invalidation splitting routine can generate a range invalidation that is split in the middle of the CONT and risk under invalidation from this errata. This condition could be triggered by a malicious userspace manipulating the TLB gathers via mmap/mprotect/munmap. Update the errata list to the include the S3 variation, detect the IOMMUs that have it, and then have SVA invalidations use a simplified version of the over invalidation algorithm from the tlbi rework series. This ensures that a single range invalidation is issued for a single MMU notifier callback and now the range invalidation is guarenteed to cover any posible CONT. Future work to add CONT to iommu_domain page tables should either use this one-invalidate/one-range invalidation algorithm or disable CONT support in the iommu_domain.

t: KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: Use kvm_s2_fault_vma_info in gmem_abort() gmem_abort() maps at s2fd->fault_ipa, which HPFAR_EL2 holds at 4K granularity whatever the page size. The generic page-table code aligns it, but pkvm_pgtable_stage2_map() looks up existing mappings over [addr, addr + size), so on a pKVM host with pages larger than 4K a guest_memfd-backed guest that faults past the first 4K of a page can find its neighbour's mapping, get -EAGAIN and take the same fault forever. The memory fault exit reports s2fd->fault_ipa too, which for a nested guest's fault is the nested IPA rather than the canonical one kvm_gmem_get_pfn() failed on. Take the addresses from kvm_s2_fault_vma_info instead, as user_mem_abort() does, and report the canonical gfn in the memory fault exit. kvm_s2_fault_get_vma_info() itself isn't called: a guest_memfd memslot's userspace_addr doesn't need to be backed by a VMA.

t: f2fs: fix to avoid folio->mapping dereference in is_{meta, node}_folio()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid folio->mapping dereference in is_{meta, node}_folio() Otherwise, it may cause NULL pointer dereference in race condition: Thread A Thread B - f2fs_setattr - f2fs_truncate - f2fs_truncate_blocks - f2fs_do_truncate_blocks - f2fs_truncate_inode_blocks - truncate_dnode - truncate_node - invalidate_mapping_pages - folio->mapping = NULL - folio_lock - is_node_folio - F2FS_F_SB(folio): dereference on folio->mapping

t: sctp: hold shkey across socket migration
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: hold shkey across socket migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers queued DATA skbs from the old socket to the new one. skb_orphan() invokes sctp_wfree() during that transfer and drops the skb-owned shared-key reference. If userspace has removed that key from the association, this can be the final reference. The following sctp_set_owner_w() then dereferences the freed chunk->shkey while trying to take the new owner reference. Take a temporary shared-key reference before orphaning the skb and release it after the new owner has taken its reference. This preserves the selected authentication key throughout the ownership transfer. Bug found and triaged by OpenAI Security Research and validated by Trail of Bits.

t: sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: sctp: re-point retained control chunks on association migration sctp_sock_migrate() transfers DATA chunk ownership but leaves retained control chunks pointing at the old socket. A later retransmission can therefore access the socket after it has been freed. Extend the migration walk to cover retained control chunks and use sctp_control_set_owner_w() to assign their new owner. Reuse the DATA ownership check so each chunk is processed once per pass, even when it is reachable through multiple lists or retained pointers. Preserve a control chunk's existing authentication key across migration so its final release can still generate SCTP_AUTH_FREE_KEY when needed.

t: platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: platform/chrome: cros_usbpd_notify: Only use drvdata when parent is GOOG0004 cros_usbpd_notify_probe_acpi() takes the EC device pointer from dev_get_drvdata(dev->parent) and assumes it is a struct cros_ec_device. That only holds when GOOG0003 is a child of GOOG0004. On older devices without that hierarchy, such as Google Nami, GOOG0003 and GOOG0004 are siblings under the ACPI EC (PNP0C09): PNP0C09:00 (acpi-ec) |-- GOOG0003:00 (cros-usbpd-notify-acpi) `-- GOOG0004:00 (cros_ec_lpcs) Before commit db65a06d10b3 ("ACPI: EC: Convert the driver to a platform one") the parent platform device had no driver data, so the driver warned and continued without an EC pointer, as intended for these devices. Since that commit the ACPI EC driver stores its struct acpi_ec there, so the driver treats a struct acpi_ec as a struct cros_ec_device and calls cros_ec_cmd() on it for every USB-C PD host event. Plugging or unplugging a charger then intermittently oopses, followed by soft lockups and a hung system: BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffffff9cf03220 #PF: supervisor write access in kernel mode Hardware name: Google Nami/Nami, BIOS 09/19/2019 Workqueue: kacpi_notify acpi_os_execute_deferred RIP: 0010:native_queued_spin_lock_slowpath+0x29d/0x330 Call Trace: _raw_spin_lock_irqsave+0x59/0x80 __mutex_lock.constprop.0+0x129/0x930 cros_ec_cmd_xfer+0x2a/0xf0 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd_xfer_status+0x1a/0x90 [cros_ec_proto] cros_ec_cmd+0xb7/0x140 [cros_ec_proto] cros_usbpd_get_event_and_notify+0x42/0xc0 [cros_usbpd_notify] acpi_ev_notify_dispatch+0x4e/0x70 acpi_os_execute_deferred+0x1a/0x30 Only read the parent's driver data when the parent's ACPI node is GOOG0004, and otherwise continue without an EC pointer. While at it, drop the reference taken by fwnode_get_parent().

t: mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/userfaultfd: only allocate anon_vma in CoW mappings find_vma_and_prepare_anon() can end up allocating an anon_vma in VMAs that are not CoW mappings, which is wrong. If we have a MAP_SHARED R/O file mapped, we lack VM_SHARED (but do have VM_MAYSHARE) and lack VM_MAYWRITE. While uffd later rejects such mappings (uffd registration requires VM_MAYWRITE, see comment in validate_dst_vma) find_vma_and_prepare_anon() still wrongly allocates an anon vma before it validates the vma. This in turn later confuses copy_page_range()->vma_needs_copy() such that we end up calling copy_hugetlb_page_range() with ranges that actually do not contain *any* per-pagetable information that would require copying, which is the basis for PMD-table sharing in the first place. copy_hugetlb_page_range() should not have to worry about shared PMD tables at all: it doesn't make any sense to copy page tables that are shared, as they can be fully recreated later. Ending up in the function with shareable page tables is the real issue. If a destination PMD table is shared in copy_hugetlb_page_range(), it might get concurrently unshared as we are not holding relevant locks, resulting in us using a page table that is no longer mapped and possibly freed after calling: dst_pte = huge_pte_alloc(dst, dst_vma, addr, sz); To fix it, do not allocate an anon_vma in non-CoW mappings and add a safety guard to copy_hugetlb_page_range(), making sure that we never end up messing with shared PMD tables in there. Before commit 867a43a34ff8a ("userfaultfd: use per-vma locks in userfaultfd operations") we would always validate the VMA before allocating an anon_vma, and consequently never wrongly allocate an anon_vma. As uffd_lock_vma() is part of the same lookup machinery and also contains a misleading VM_SHARED check, change that one as well directly for consistency. A follow-up cleanup will stop taking the hugetlb_vma_lock_read(src_vma) lock in copy_hugetlb_page_range() entirely. Further, the usage of VM_SHARED in userfaultfd code should be cleaned up later to focus on CoW vs. non-CoW mappings.

t: mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: mm/shmem: honour F_SEAL_EXEC when an ACL is set The owner of a memfd sealed with F_SEAL_EXEC can still change its execute bits by setting a POSIX access ACL. With CONFIG_TMPFS_POSIX_ACL, this lets an unprivileged owner make a non-executable memfd executable, bypassing vm.memfd_noexec=2. simple_set_acl() updates i_mode directly, bypassing the seal check in shmem_setattr(). Add shmem_set_acl() to check the resulting mode. Share the F_SEAL_EXEC check with shmem_setattr() using memfd_check_seals_mode() in include/linux/memfd.h. Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private. [ david: use common helper; simplify description ]

t: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: route bmc frames via the high queue only for DTIM delivery In AP mode every broadcast and multicast data frame is routed to TX_DESC_QSEL_HIGH, the after-DTIM queue, whether or not anybody is asleep. The firmware drains that queue at beacon pace, a dozen or so frames per second measured on RTL8822BU, while one associated client's mDNS/SSDP chatter alone exceeds that. The excess accumulates inside the chip until the shared TX page pool is exhausted (measured: 14 of 1803 pages left). From that point every host-sourced frame queues behind the backlog: authentication responses reach the air seconds after the client has given up, so no station can associate anymore, and the beacon reserved-page download fails the BCN_VALID poll ("error beacon valid") because it needs pages from the same pool. The AP keeps beaconing, so the failure looks like a silent RX stall and only a reboot recovers. mac80211 already decides when after-DTIM delivery is needed: it sets IEEE80211_TX_CTL_SEND_AFTER_DTIM on bmc frames only while at least one station is actually dozing. Honor that instead of routing unconditionally: flagged frames keep going through the high queue with the MORE_DATA and HGQMD handling introduced by commit 076f786a0ae1 ("wifi: rtw88: Fix AP mode incorrect DTIM behavior"), everything else leaves at line rate through the AC queues. This partially reverts the usb.c hunk of that commit, whose unconditional routing is what lets the backlog build up. On a bench AP (USB2, 20 MHz, WPA2, hostapd, a Windows client driven through disconnect/reconnect cycles): reconnects fail 0/5 on RTL8822BU and 0/3 on RTL8821CU before this change, and pass 10/10 and 5/5 with it, with the page pool staying healthy and no beacon errors logged.

t: wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: wifi: rtw88: usb: bound what the driver feeds the after-DTIM queue Frames routed to the high queue are transmitted right after DTIM beacons only, inside the ATIM window, while they wait in the shared TX page pool. The driver puts no limit on how many it hands over, so as long as one station dozes, any sustained broadcast or multicast traffic outruns the drain and empties the pool: measured on an RTL8822BU AP with a single client in power save and ~40 frames/s of mDNS chatter, the free page count at 0x240 goes from 1803 to 16 in about 100 seconds and stays there for as long as the traffic lasts. From that point every other transmit queues behind the backlog, authentication responses arrive too late for anyone to join, and the reserved page download fails ("error beacon valid"). The AP keeps beaconing and only a reboot recovers. Feed the high queue through a small budget that refills below the measured drain rate (about 3 frames per DTIM, ~15/s at dtim_period 2 on the default 2 TU ATIM window); whatever exceeds the budget leaves on its access category queue right away. The high queue backlog is now bounded by the burst size under any load, so the page pool cannot run dry, at the price that a dozing station may miss part of a broadcast storm.

t: f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: zone: fix to avoid bio split on sequential zone In the block layer, bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio if it exceeds any underlying queue limits: 1. queue_max_sectors: Splits bios larger than the transfer limit. This limit is set by the device driver/DMA controller (max_hw_sectors) and device-mapper targets. When flushing dirty pages (governed by VFS writeback_chunk_size() and f2fs nr_pages_to_skip()), f2fs merges contiguous pages into bios up to 512KB (1024 sectors) or more without checking queue_max_sectors, which will be split if the device or DM target enforces a smaller limit. 2. queue_max_segments: Splits bios exceeding scatter-gather segment limits. f2fs allocates bios with up to 256 pages, exceeding the 128-segment limit of DM targets (dm-default-key/dm-crypt) if pages are discontiguous. 3. chunk_sectors: Splits bios crossing chunk/zone boundaries. In f2fs, section_size strictly matches zone_size, and block allocation never spans across section boundaries, so bios never cross chunk_sectors. Crucially, when bio_split_to_limits() splits a bio, bio_submit_split() submits the tail half via submit_bio_noacct() before returning the head half to the caller. On a sequential zoned device, this causes the tail bio to arrive at the zone write plug before the head: dm-3: zone 7: prepare_bio wp mismatch: bio sector 30720 offset 2048 != wp_offset 248, len 248 The write plug rejects the out-of-order tail with BLK_STS_IOERR, causing f2fs_stop_checkpoint() and remounting the filesystem read-only: 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725678+08:00 localhost kernel: CPU: 9 UID: 0 PID: 243 Comm: kworker/9:1H Not tainted 6.12.81-gb3ef518fb26d #5 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725750+08:00 localhost kernel: Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS 1.17.0-debian-1.17.0-1 04/01/2014 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725753+08:00 localhost kernel: Workqueue: dm-3_zwplugs blk_zone_wplug_bio_work 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725756+08:00 localhost kernel: Call Trace: 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725758+08:00 localhost kernel: <TASK> 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725758+08:00 localhost kernel: dump_stack_lvl+0x4d/0x70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725759+08:00 localhost kernel: f2fs_stop_checkpoint+0x1df/0x5d0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725759+08:00 localhost kernel: ? blk_zone_wplug_bio_work+0x4eb/0x740 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725760+08:00 localhost kernel: f2fs_cache_write_end_io+0x545/0x6e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725761+08:00 localhost kernel: blk_zone_wplug_bio_work+0x4eb/0x740 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725762+08:00 localhost kernel: process_one_work+0x5c6/0xde0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725764+08:00 localhost kernel: ? assign_work+0x124/0x4e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725765+08:00 localhost kernel: worker_thread+0x403/0xb70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725765+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __kthread_parkme+0x82/0x140 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725766+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_worker_thread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725766+08:00 localhost kernel: kthread+0x235/0x2e0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725767+08:00 localhost kernel: ? recalc_sigpending+0x128/0x1d0 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725767+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725769+08:00 localhost kernel: ret_from_fork+0x2f/0x70 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725769+08:00 localhost kernel: ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725770+08:00 localhost kernel: ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725771+08:00 localhost kernel: </TASK> 2026-09-30T22:09:23.725771+08:00 localhost kernel: F2FS-fs (dm-0): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 3 To prevent write bios destined for sequential zones from being split: 1. In __bio_alloc(), bound npages to bdev_max_segments(bdev) for writes to sequential zone areas. 2. In page_is_mergeable(), check queue_max_segments() and queue_max_sectors() for sequential zone areas, so f2fs will not merge beyond the queue limits.

t: f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: return -EIO for a lost inode block after cp_error After cp_error, dirty node caches are dropped without being written. If such an inode was never written, its NAT entry is still NEW_ADDR, and reading its inode block returns -ENOENT. f2fs_get_dnode_of_data() passes that -ENOENT up, and callers take it as a hole. Since the inode block is missing, the next offset can only advance one block, so fiemap walks block by block up to maxbytes, about 2^30 blocks, while holding the inode lock. It took hours in a power-off recovery test after shutdown and blocked unlink and umount on the file. Return -EIO instead of -ENOENT when the inode block itself is missing after cp_error or shutdown. A missing direct or indirect node is still reported as -ENOENT.

t: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: bound the SIT/NAT bitmaps by the checkpoint pack sit_ver_bitmap_bytesize and nat_ver_bitmap_bytesize are used as memcpy lengths into and out of sbi->ckpt, which is sized from cp_payload alone, and nothing compares either length against that allocation. sanity_check_ckpt() has checked these two fields since c77ec61ca0a4, which added them after a crafted image overran build_sit_info(). That check ties each length to a segment count; it never compares either against the allocation, which is the half this adds. Mounting over-reads in build_sit_info() and build_node_manager(), and the first checkpoint writes the same lengths back through the same pointers, so the over-read's contents reach the on-disk checkpoint. An unmount is enough; the filesystem does not have to be used. Bound both ends the way __bitmap_ptr() lays them out. The three branches differ, so a single sum of the two lengths would still admit a small overflow when cp_payload is non-zero.

t: KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: KVM: arm64: vgic: Stop the target vcpu when disabling LPIs Disabling LPIs is pretty nasty, as it directly messes with the AP list of the affected CPU, which could be running... This has the potential to lead to really bad behaviours, and we should not be doing that. Take example on the way the Active state is handled and simply pause the the vcpu so that we are sure it is in a quiescent state, and the state be safely manipulated. Nobody has any expectation of performance for this anyway.

t: f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect()
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to avoid potential reference count leak in do_garbage_collect() In do_garbage_collect(), we have reserved reference counts on summary cache of all segments, once gc_thread encounter freezing, we need to release all reference counts.

t: nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: nvme-tcp: Validate the queue state under the queue lock in the address attribute Reading the "address" sysfs attribute calls kernel_getsockname() on the admin queue socket, which can race with the queue teardown during connection error recovery: a reader can observe NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE set, then block on the queue lock while nvme_tcp_free_queue() releases the socket and clears queue->sock without holding the lock. Once the reader acquires the lock it dereferences the NULL socket pointer. Commit 76d54bf20cdc ("nvme-tcp: don't access released socket during error recovery") had the queue liveness check inside the lock. Commit 782373ba2766 ("nvme: tcp: avoid race between queue_lock lock and destroy") moved it back out because the lock itself is destroyed in nvme_tcp_free_queue(), so a reader arriving late trips mutex_destroy(). Check the queue liveness inside the queue lock, and clear queue->sock under the same lock. The teardown clears NVME_TCP_Q_LIVE under the lock well before the socket is released, so a reader either sees the bit cleared or a socket that cannot be released while it holds the lock. To also close the lock lifetime race, the queue locks are now owned by the controller: they are initialized with the queue array and only destroyed when the controller is freed, which cannot happen while a sysfs attribute read is still in progress. The queue count is computed by the NVME_TCP_OPT_NR_QUEUES() macro from the original connect options for both initialization and destruction, as reconnects may shrink ctrl->queue_count.

t: f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: fix to invalidate curseg if change_curseg() fails Our consistency stress test (fsstress + fio + atomic write workers + "f2fs_io shutdown 1") triggers below kernel BUG: F2FS-fs (vdd): Stopped filesystem due to reason: 0 ------------[ cut here ]------------ kernel BUG at fs/f2fs/segment.c:3989! Oops: invalid opcode: 0000 [#1] SMP KASAN PTI Workqueue: writeback wb_workfn (flush-253:48) RIP: 0010:f2fs_allocate_data_block+0x257a/0x38e0 Call Trace: <TASK> do_write_block+0x155/0xc10 f2fs_outplace_write_data+0x192/0x340 f2fs_do_write_data_page+0xc57/0x1880 f2fs_write_single_data_page+0xda9/0x15a0 f2fs_write_cache_pages+0x973/0x1f20 __f2fs_write_data_pages+0x6c4/0x1890 do_writepages+0x21e/0x560 __writeback_single_inode+0x119/0x11b0 writeback_sb_inodes+0x67d/0x17a0 wb_writeback+0x207/0x820 wb_workfn+0x128/0xc30 process_one_work+0x925/0x1600 worker_thread+0x60a/0xff0 kthread+0x35f/0x460 ret_from_fork+0x474/0x7e0 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30 </TASK> The BUG is f2fs_bug_on(sbi, curseg->next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG(sbi)) in f2fs_allocate_data_block(), next_blkoff was 512. The root cause is a race in between atomic write commit and shutdown as below: Thread A (commit atomic write) Thread B (shutdown) Thread C (writeback) - f2fs_ioc_commit_atomic_write - f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __f2fs_commit_atomic_write - __replace_atomic_write_block - f2fs_replace_block - __f2fs_replace_block - f2fs_ioc_shutdown - f2fs_do_shutdown : F2FS_GOING_DOWN_METASYNC - f2fs_sync_fs - f2fs_write_single_data_page : pass f2fs_cp_error() check - f2fs_stop_checkpoint : set CP_ERROR_FLAG - change_curseg - reset_curseg : curseg->segno = new_segno : curseg->alloc_type = SSR : curseg->next_blkoff = __next_free_blkoff() which is BLKS_PER_SEG if there is no free slot in new_segno - f2fs_get_sum_cache : return -EIO due to f2fs_cp_error() : return error w/o restoring curseg : goto out_unlock, skip restoring old segno, blkoff and alloc_type - f2fs_do_write_data_page - f2fs_outplace_write_data - do_write_block - f2fs_allocate_data_block : curseg->segno is valid : f2fs_bug_on(next_blkoff >= BLKS_PER_SEG) Since commit 86f33603f8c5 ("f2fs: handle errors of f2fs_get_meta_page_nofail"), change_curseg() can fail after the curseg has already been switched to the new segment, then the curseg is left in an inconsistent state: it points to a segment which may have no free slot, its summary block is zeroed, and the caller can not restore it. Subsequent block allocation on the curseg will trigger the BUG. Moreover, the writeback thread dies with curseg_lock, curseg_mutex and sentry_lock held, so the commit, shutdown and other I/O threads hang in D state. Since change_curseg() only fails once CP_ERROR_FLAG is set, no checkpoint will be committed afterward, let's invalidate the curseg via reset_curseg_fields() on failure, as new_curseg() does for -ENOSPC, then f2fs_allocate_data_block() will fail with -ENOSPC on the curseg instead of triggering BUG, and do_write_block() can handle the error since CP_ERROR_FLA ---truncated---

t: f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: f2fs: release a removed xattr node in roll-forward recovery When xattrs shrink enough to fit in the inline xattr area, write_all_xattrs() truncates the xattr node and clears i_xattr_nid. If the file is then fsynced without a checkpoint, only the inode block is written, with i_xattr_nid of 0. Roll-forward recovery starts from the checkpointed inode, whose i_xattr_nid still points to the old xattr node. f2fs_recover_inline_xattr() copies only the inline xattr area, and f2fs_update_inode() writes the old i_xattr_nid back. So the inode keeps the stale xattr node: - The node block is never released, and fsck reports "nonzero bytes in xattr space after end of list". - If the inline xattr list ends exactly at the end of the inline area, its terminator is read from the stale node, and the removed xattrs come back after recovery. When the fsynced inode has no xattr node but the checkpointed one has, release the old xattr node as truncate_node() does: check its block address, invalidate the block and drop its node cache, which may still be dirty.

t: iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: iommufd/iova_bitmap: Ensure that iova_bitmap_set() handles the full IOVA Generally userspace is going to step the dirty bitmap through the IOVA space. However if the bitmap ends in the middle of a large PTE this is problematic. The first step will clear the dirty bit and report dirty to the end of its bitmap while the second step will see the clear'd dirty and report clean for the start of the bitmap. If it happens this ends up losing dirties. Further this function is missing bounds checking so if this does happen ther is a good chance it will write memory beyond what the userspace was expecting. Return an error code if this illegal condition happens.

t: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment, assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a shortcut to a pair of new nodes. If the node is itself the target of a shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node, and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects: assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion. Deletion gets a node there. When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment. The next key that shares it too takes this path. Eighteen insertions and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees with the sixteen. Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well. assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in excised_meta[]. The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did. Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

t: assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure
d: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved: assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree. Where the copy reaches a shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(), fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then allocates the copy of the node after it. The memcpy() leaves the new shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on the old node's back pointer fires. Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated. A copied shortcut is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there to follow it. Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the trees gc builds are the same as before. Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation fail in turn.

t: Crun: crun: tmpcopyup follows a second path lookup and copies image files onto the host
d: A flaw was found in crun. When copying files onto a tmpfs mounted with tmpcopyup, crun opens the destination a second time by name. A container that shares a writable volume with the container being created can change that path between the two lookups, so crun copies image files onto host files, including files under /proc/sys.

t: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: org.keycloak:keycloak-common: uma uri suffix matching authorization bypass
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When evaluating access permissions, Keycloak Authorization Services improperly matches resource paths containing wildcard file extensions by evaluating only the file extension suffix and ignoring configured path prefixes. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by requesting a restricted resource that shares a file extension with a more permissive resource, leading to an authorization bypass and unintended access to protected data.

t: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: post-logout redirect uri configuration of a disabled client is still honored, leading to open redirect
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. The OpenID Connect (OIDC) logout endpoint continues to honor post-logout redirect rules for disabled clients rather than rejecting the requests. If a disabled client retains permissive redirect configurations, a remote attacker can exploit this issue by supplying an arbitrary redirection target in a logout request, leading to an open redirect that can be used in phishing attacks.

t: Hawtio: hawtio-systems: quadratic redos in flightrecordingdownloadfacade request-uri pattern
d: A flaw was found in Hawtio. An authenticated remote attacker can cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by sending a specially crafted request URI to monitored endpoints. The FlightRecordingDownloadFacade servlet filter uses an inefficient regular expression pattern that causes catastrophic backtracking when processing certain long requests. This issue leads to excessive CPU utilization, causing handling threads to hang and degrading service availability.

An uncontrolled recursion vulnerability exists in the LINE iOS app prior to version 26.19.0. The Flex Message processing component does not adequately validate the structure of externally supplied message content. As a result, an attacker who is able to send a crafted message to a victim could cause the application to crash when the message is received or displayed. A server-side mitigation has been deployed that also protects existing iOS clients that have not been updated to version 26.19.0.

t: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: org.keycloak:keycloak-server-spi-private: account resource sharing grants scopes outside the resource definition
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. The Account API endpoint for sharing resources fails to verify whether owner-managed access is enabled and accepts permission scopes not assigned to the resource. An authenticated user can exploit this vulnerability to generate pre-granted permission tickets, causing Keycloak to bypass policy evaluation and issue access tokens with unauthorized scopes.

t: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: uma issues fresh rpts for disabled resource-server clients
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When processing token requests using the User-Managed Access (UMA) grant, Keycloak fails to verify whether a target client or resource server is enabled before issuing an authorization token. An authenticated remote user can exploit this flaw to obtain valid Requesting Party Tokens (RPTs) for disabled clients, bypassing administrative access controls and permissions restrictions.

t: Org.keycloak.services.resources: client minimum acr (level of authentication) is not enforced when the login starts at the credential reset endpoint, allowing a
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When a client application enforces step-up authentication or multi-factor authentication (MFA) via a minimum authentication level, Keycloak fails to apply this requirement to login sessions initiated through the credential reset endpoint. An attacker who possesses a user's initial credentials (such as a password) can navigate from the reset interface back to the standard login form and authenticate without completing the required second factor. This flaw allows an attacker to obtain valid access tokens and gain unauthorized access to protected services without satisfying mandatory security controls.

t: Org.keycloak:keycloak-services: pre-revocation id tokens can mint fresh uma rpts after realm not-before
d: A flaw was found in Keycloak. When an administrator revokes tokens by setting a not-before revocation cutoff, Keycloak fails to enforce this boundary when processing User-Managed Access (UMA) grant requests using ID token claims. An authenticated remote user with an active session can submit a previously revoked ID token to receive a fresh Requesting Party Token (RPT). This flaw allows an attacker to bypass token revocation and retain unauthorized access to protected resources.

t: BeamNG.drive before 0.40.6 LuaJIT FFI Sandbox Escape via JIT Bounds-Check Bypass
d: BeamNG.drive before 0.40.6 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability because JIT-compiled LuaJIT traces omit FFI array bounds checks, letting untrusted Lua escape the sandbox. Attackers supplying a malicious mod can JIT-compile an FFI store loop, write out of range using a tostring() address leak, re-enable ffi.load, and run commands as the game user.

t: lwext4 through 1.0.0 Heap Buffer Overflow via ext4_fs_init_inode_bitmap
d: lwext4 through 1.0.0 contains a heap buffer overflow in ext4_fs_init_inode_bitmap() in src/ext4_fs.c because it does not validate s_inodes_per_group against the inode bitmap size. Attackers can supply a crafted ext4 image with an oversized s_inodes_per_group so memset writes past the heap buffer, corrupting memory and crashing the mounting application.

t: lwext4 through 1.0.0 Out-of-Bounds Write via ext4_fs_init_block_bitmap
d: lwext4 through 1.0.0 contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in ext4_fs_init_block_bitmap() that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory via crafted superblock geometry fields. Attackers can supply an ext4 image with oversized s_reserved_gdt_blocks and BLOCK_UNINIT groups to write past the bitmap buffer, crashing applications that mount it.

t: Dokploy 0.28.0 before 0.31.1 Path Traversal via patch.readRepoDirectories repoPath
d: Dokploy 0.28.0 before 0.31.1 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the patch.readRepoDirectories tRPC procedure that allows authenticated organization members to list tracked files of arbitrary git repositories. Attackers with service read permission can supply a crafted repoPath, which is passed to git ls-tree unconfined, to enumerate other organizations' application and compose source trees.

t: FFmpeg 7.0 through 9.0.2 Out-of-Bounds Read via dvdvideo_menu_next_ps_block()
d: FFmpeg 7.0 through 9.0.2 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in dvdvideo_menu_next_ps_block() in libavformat/dvdvideodec.c when demuxing DVD menu domains. Attackers can craft a DVD image whose last cell sector and NAV next-VOBU pointer bypass the end-of-cell check, overreading pgc->cell_playback and crashing the process.

t: Bar Assistant 3.0.0 before 6.11.0 Authorization Bypass via Null Invite Code
d: Bar Assistant 3.0.0 before 6.11.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in BarController::join that allows authenticated users to join bars without a valid invite code. Attackers can send POST requests to /api/bars/join omitting invite_code, matching invite-disabled bars with NULL codes, to read cocktails, ingredients, members, settings and search tokens.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via a declared element length passed unchecked to sysread in asn_read and asn_get. The length an element declares in its BER header is passed to sysread as the read size. Perl grows the target buffer to that size before reading, so memory is allocated from the declared length, not from the data received. A 6-byte header can declare a length of up to 4GB. A single header makes the reading process allocate the declared size. Where the allocation fails, perl exits with "Out of memory", which eval cannot catch.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unbounded arc length in OBJECT IDENTIFIER decoding and encoding. The content of an OBJECT IDENTIFIER or RELATIVE-OID element is passed to unpack "w*" on decode, and the arcs of an OID string to pack "w*" on encode. Perl converts each arc to or from its decimal string in time quadratic in the arc's length, and nothing limits that length. An attacker who controls the decoded data, or an OID string passed to encode, can exhaust CPU with a single oversized arc.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unlimited recursion depth in constructed-form string decoding. Any constructed-form string element causes the decoder to recurse on the element's contents. The BER encoding controls nesting depth at four bytes per level, with no bound checked. Perl recursion is heap-allocated, so the process grows without a stack crash. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a small deeply nested constructed string.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via zero-length BIT STRING content. A BIT STRING with zero content octets passes -1 to substr as the length. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the decoded value is nearly all of the input that follows the element. In the constructed form each zero-length segment copies the rest of the input again, so memory grows with the square of the input size. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust memory with a short constructed BIT STRING. The resulting value also contains bytes from adjacent input.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via exponent-notation string in INTEGER encoding. The encoder routes any value with abs >= 2**31 to i2osp without validating that it is an integer. A string in exponent notation such as "1e8000" passes that threshold. Math::BigInt expands it to an 8001-digit integer, and i2osp's per-octet conversion loop is quadratic in that size. An attacker who controls encoded INTEGER values can exhaust CPU with a short exponent-notation string.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding. Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. For a minimal one-byte binary REAL, the exponent byte is read from outside the element, making the mantissa length -1. Perl reads a negative length as an offset from the end of the string, so the mantissa is nearly all of the input that follows the element. The long-form exponent path also omits the extra length octet when sizing the mantissa. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a list of such values, as each mantissa loop iterates over the remaining input. The decoded values are also computed from bytes outside each element.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv. asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles. A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.

t: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip
d: Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic bigint loop in os2ip. Every INTEGER or ENUMERATED longer than four content octets reaches os2ip, which iterates over each content octet with $result = ($result * 256) + $octet. Each multiplication operates on a bigint that grows by one octet per step, so decoding an n-octet value takes O(n^2) bigint work. Nothing limits content length before this loop runs. An attacker who controls the decoded data can exhaust CPU with a single oversized INTEGER or ENUMERATED value.

t: aoiflux mutant Forensic hive_builtins.go memory allocation
